solution.concept_anchor: Nilgiri Tahr vs Nilgiri Langur IUCN status; caecilian taxonomy
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a swaps Nilgiri Tahr (EN) with Nilgiri Langur (VU), exploiting the name similarity between the two Nilgiri species.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Purple Frog — it is Endangered (EN) and sole member of Nasikabatrachidae; eliminate options pairing it with VU.
Distinguish Nilgiri Tahr (EN) from Nilgiri Langur (VU) — both are Western Ghats endemics but with different statuses; the Tahr is the mountain ungulate (EN) while Langur is the primate (VU).
Confirm Lion-Tailed Macaque = EN (not CR); eliminate any option assigning it CR.
Ichthyophis (caecilian) = amphibian (not reptile) found in Northeast India — confirm this pairing and select option b (A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Nilgiri Tahr vs Nilgiri Langur swap is a classic entity-swap trap — both are Western Ghats endemics with 'Nilgiri' in their names. Nilgiri Tahr (Nilgiritragus hylocrius) is an ungulate classified as EN; Nilgiri Langur (Semnopithecus johnii) is a primate classified as VU. Students who know one status may apply it to the wrong Nilgiri species. Additionally, the Ichthyophis-amphibian pairing tests whether students know caecilians are amphibians, not reptiles.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests species-specific IUCN status and taxonomic classification for Western Ghats and Northeast India species.

Correct pairings:
• A (Nilgiri Tahr) — 2 (Endangered): Nilgiritragus hylocrius, the Western Ghats mountain ungulate, is IUCN EN. Found in the Nilgiri Hills and southern Western Ghats above 1,200m.
• B (Lion-Tailed Macaque) — 4 (Endangered): Macaca silenus is IUCN EN, endemic to Western Ghats — found in Silent Valley, Anamalai Hills, Kalakad-Mundanthurai. Not Himalayan.
• C (Nilgiri Langur) — 1 (Vulnerable): Semnopithecus johnii is IUCN VU — a primate, unlike the Nilgiri Tahr which is an ungulate. Both are Western Ghats endemics with different threat levels.
• D (Ichthyophis sp.) — 3 (Amphibian — Caecilian): Ichthyophis is a caecilian (legless, limbless amphibian) found in Northeast India. It is NOT a reptile — a common taxonomic trap.

Value Addition:
• Nilgiri Tahr is the state animal of Tamil Nadu.
• Lion-Tailed Macaque is one of the rarest and most endangered primates in the world — estimated at fewer than 4,000 individuals.
• India has over 50 caecilian species — mostly in Northeast India and Western Ghats; all are burrowing, limbless amphibians.

solution.concept_anchor: Sariska and Panna — local extinction and tiger reintroduction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct, R explains A) is deceptive for students who know poaching caused Sariska's local extinction and assume corridor isolation is the explanation — but R says 'corridor isolation,' which is a different (structural) cause from poaching (the proximate cause).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Sariska and Panna Tiger Reserves experienced local extinction of tigers in the 2000s before reintroduction efforts: Yes, Sariska (2004–05) and Panna (2009) confirmed local tiger extinctions.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Both reserves suffered from corridor isolation that prevented natural recolonisation from adjacent tiger populations: Yes, both reserves are geographically isolated with no connected source populations — this is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — The local extinctions at Sariska (caused primarily by poaching) and Panna (combination of poaching and prey depletion) were the proximate causes; corridor isolation explains why natural recovery did not occur after extinction, not why extinction happened. However, R is presented as explaining the occurrence of local extinction — corridor isolation as a vulnerability factor is a contributing but not the primary explanation for why extinction occurred. R explains post-extinction dynamics more than the extinction event itself.
A correct + R correct + R is a contributing but not the primary causal explanation → option b (both correct, R NOT the correct explanation).
solution.final_explanation:
Sariska and Panna are India's two most documented cases of local tiger extinction followed by managed reintroduction.

Assertion (A): Both Sariska (2004–05) and Panna (2009) lost their entire tiger populations before reintroduction programmes — Correct. Sariska's extinction was confirmed by camera trap surveys; Panna's was reported by the Wildlife Institute of India.

Reason (R): Corridor isolation prevented natural recolonisation — Correct. Both reserves are geographically isolated: Sariska (Rajasthan) lacks functional connectivity to Ranthambore or other populations; Panna (Madhya Pradesh) is similarly isolated. This meant that even after conditions improved, tigers could not return naturally.

Causal analysis: R explains why natural recovery was impossible after extinction, not why extinction occurred in the first place. Sariska's extinction was caused by poaching enabled by governance failure; Panna's by a combination of poaching and prey depletion. Corridor isolation made recovery impossible, but it was not the direct cause of the extinction event.

Conclusion: A correct, R correct, but R explains the structural vulnerability and post-extinction constraint, not the primary cause of local extinction → Option b.

Value Addition:
• Tigers from Ranthambore (Rajasthan) were used to restock Sariska; from Kanha and Pench for Panna.
• Sariska is located in the Aravalli range — its isolation is due to agricultural and urban expansion fragmenting the landscape.
• Critically Tiger Endangered Landscapes (CTELs) were identified specifically to address connectivity-based extinction risks.

solution.concept_anchor: National Wildlife Action Plan 2017–2031 and HWC compensation state subject

statement_analysis.statement: The National Wildlife Action Plan (2017–2031) explicitly identifies human-wildlife conflict as a priority area and provides for a uniform national compensation scheme administered by the Central Government.
statement_analysis.reason: While the National Wildlife Action Plan (2017–2031) does identify HWC as a priority, compensation for wildlife attacks is administered by State Wildlife Boards under respective state schemes — there is no uniform national compensation scheme administered by the Central Government.

statement_analysis.statement: The Leopard (Panthera pardus), while classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, is associated with the highest incidence of human-wildlife conflict among large carnivores in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Leopard is IUCN VU and generates the most human-wildlife conflict incidents in India due to its adaptability to peri-urban landscapes — particularly evident in areas like Mumbai's Aarey Colony and parts of Uttarakhand.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 62 of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, the state government of a coastal state can independently declare a Schedule I marine species as vermin within its territorial waters without requiring Central Government approval.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 62 vests the vermin declaration power in the Central Government — state governments cannot independently make such declarations even for species in their territorial waters, particularly for Schedule I species.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (2 only) is the correct answer; wait — re-evaluating: Statement 1 is incorrect, Statement 2 is correct, Statement 3 is incorrect. So only Statement 2 is correct → option b. Rechecking options: (a) 1 and 2 only, (b) 2 only, (c) 2 and 3 only, (d) 1, 2 and 3. Correct answer should be b.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — the NWAP does prioritise HWC, but the claim of a 'uniform national compensation scheme by Central Government' is a scope-extension error; compensation is state-administered; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Leopard as highest-conflict large carnivore, IUCN VU, is a documented conservation-conflict fact; Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Section 62 vermin power vests centrally regardless of territorial domain; states cannot act independently for Schedule I species; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is correct — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 adds 'uniform national compensation scheme administered by the Central Government' to the true fact that NWAP 2017–2031 addresses HWC. This scope-extension makes the statement sound like a logical policy progression — if HWC is a national priority, surely a national compensation scheme follows. But compensation is a state subject under WPA — state wildlife boards run their own schemes with different rates, coverage, and procedures.
solution.final_explanation:
Human-wildlife conflict policy in India operates through both national frameworks and state-level implementation — a distinction that generates frequent MCQ traps.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: National Wildlife Action Plan (2017–2031) does prioritise HWC, but compensation administration is decentralised. States like Maharashtra, Uttarakhand, and Karnataka have their own ex-gratia compensation rates for crop damage, livestock loss, and human injury/death. No centralised uniform national scheme exists under WPA.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Leopard generates the most conflict incidents partly because of its ability to thrive in degraded and peri-urban habitats. Mumbai's Sanjay Gandhi National Park–adjacent areas and Uttarakhand's hill districts record consistent leopard attacks.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Section 62's vermin declaration power remains with the Central Government even for marine species. State governments can petition for such declarations but cannot act unilaterally, especially for Schedule I species.

Value Addition:
• India's tiger conflict incidents are relatively fewer because tigers primarily inhabit forest interiors; leopards' edge-habitat preference explains higher conflict rates.
• HWC mitigation tools include: early warning systems, predator-proof enclosures, insurance schemes, and rapid response teams.
• Leopard is also on Schedule I of WPA — making its conflict resolution legally complex.

solution.concept_anchor: Sea turtle IUCN status hierarchy — from most to least threatened
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c places Green Turtle before Hawksbill, which a student who knows Green Turtle is Endangered might rank above Hawksbill if they have not specifically confirmed Hawksbill = CR.
elimination_logic: The question asks for sequence from most threatened to least threatened by IUCN status.
Confirm Hawksbill = CR (most threatened among Indian sea turtles) — it comes first.
Confirm Green Turtle = EN (second most threatened) — it comes second.
Confirm Leatherback = VU and Olive Ridley = VU — both are Vulnerable; among the two VU species, sequence by Indian conservation significance (Leatherback is larger and has more restricted nesting).
Correct sequence: Hawksbill (CR) → Green (EN) → Leatherback (VU) → Olive Ridley (VU) = option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here operates as a status-level swap. Students who know three of the four statuses but confuse Hawksbill (CR) with Endangered may sequence Hawksbill second, choosing option c. Hawksbill's CR status is specifically testable — it is the rarest sea turtle nesting in India and its shell-based trade history makes it globally the most threatened.
solution.final_explanation:
India hosts all five sea turtle species, each with a distinct IUCN status. Sequencing from most to least threatened:

1. Hawksbill Sea Turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) — Critically Endangered (CR): Most threatened; historically targeted for 'tortoiseshell' products; nests on Andaman coasts.
2. Green Sea Turtle (Chelonia mydas) — Endangered (EN): Faces threats from bycatch and habitat loss; nests on Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar.
3. Leatherback Sea Turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) — Vulnerable (VU): World's largest turtle; nests on Great Nicobar Island primarily.
4. Olive Ridley Sea Turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea) — Vulnerable (VU): Most abundant; famous for mass nesting (arribada) at Gahirmatha, Rushikulya.

(Loggerhead, the fifth species, is also VU but rarely nests in India.)

Wrong options fail because they misplace Hawksbill (not EN) or Green Turtle (not CR) or conflate the two VU species.

Value Addition:
• Gahirmatha Marine Sanctuary (Odisha) protects the world's largest Olive Ridley rookery.
• Mechanised fishing trawlers without Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs) are the primary threat to sea turtles in Indian waters.
• IUCN Loggerhead status: Vulnerable — least commonly documented in India.

solution.concept_anchor: Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve — Western Ghats endemic hotspot
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Nokrek — Assam) is deceptive because Nokrek is associated with Northeast India and students may vaguely associate it with Assam (a major Northeast state) rather than its correct location in Meghalaya.
elimination_logic: Verify option a — Nokrek Biosphere Reserve is in Meghalaya (Garo Hills), not Assam; option a is incorrectly matched.

Verify option b — Simlipal is in Odisha (correct), but it is associated with Tigers and Elephants as a UNESCO WNBR site; the description 'gene sanctuary for sal forests' is not its primary classification; option b needs verification — Simlipal is indeed WNBR-recognised but not specifically a 'gene sanctuary'; option b may be plausible.

Verify option c — Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve spans Kerala and Tamil Nadu and is specifically known for its endemic plant and animal species, particularly in the Western Ghats; this is correctly matched.
Verify option d — Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve is UNESCO-recognised but it is a marine-terrestrial ecosystem, not primarily a freshwater biodiversity hotspot; option d is imprecise.
Select option c — Agasthyamalai correctly paired with Western Ghats endemic species hotspot.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap places Nokrek in Assam (option a) to exploit students' geographic association of Northeast biodiversity with Assam, which is the most prominent Northeast state in conservation discourse. Nokrek is actually in Meghalaya's Garo Hills — home to wild citrus relatives. This is a precise geography fact that separates well-prepared students from those with superficial coverage.
solution.final_explanation:
Biosphere Reserves require precise state-location and thematic-role knowledge.

• Option (a) Nokrek Biosphere Reserve — Assam: Incorrectly matched. Nokrek is in Meghalaya (Garo Hills district), not Assam. It is a UNESCO WNBR site and is the gene sanctuary for wild citrus relatives (Citrus indica).
• Option (b) Simlipal Biosphere Reserve — primary habitat for Bengal Tiger and Indian Elephant in Odisha: Partially correct location (Odisha), but Simlipal is not specifically described as a 'gene sanctuary for sal forests' as its primary designation — it is a tiger and elephant reserve that is also UNESCO WNBR-recognised; this pairing requires context verification.
• Option (c) Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve — Western Ghats endemic species hotspot (Kerala-Tamil Nadu): Correctly matched. Agasthyamalai is a UNESCO WNBR-recognised biosphere reserve spanning the Agasthyamalai Hills in southern Kerala and Tamil Nadu, known for exceptional endemic biodiversity including rare orchids and medicinal plants.
• Option (d) Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve — UNESCO-recognised for freshwater biodiversity: Incorrectly characterised. Great Nicobar is known for its tropical marine and forest ecosystems, including Leatherback Sea Turtle nesting, not primarily for freshwater biodiversity.

Value Addition:
• Agasthyamalai contains the Kalakad-Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve within its core zone.
• Simlipal Biosphere Reserve (Odisha) was added to UNESCO WNBR in 2009.

solution.concept_anchor: CITES Appendix I species — Tiger, Elephant, Rhino; Rosewood plant listing

statement_analysis.statement: The Bengal Tiger (Panthera tigris tigris) is listed under CITES Appendix I, prohibiting all commercial international trade.
statement_analysis.reason: All tiger subspecies are listed under CITES Appendix I. Commercial trade in tigers and tiger parts is absolutely prohibited under CITES.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Elephant (Elephas maximus) is listed under CITES Appendix II, allowing regulated commercial trade in elephant products including ivory.
statement_analysis.reason: Indian Elephant (and all Asian Elephants) are listed under CITES Appendix I, not Appendix II. Commercial trade is prohibited. India has consistently opposed any downlisting to Appendix II and has opposed proposals at CITES CoP to allow African elephant ivory trade.

statement_analysis.statement: Indian Rosewood (Dalbergia sissoo) was listed under CITES Appendix II in 2017, demonstrating that CITES coverage extends to plant species.
statement_analysis.reason: India listed Indian Rosewood under CITES Appendix II at CoP17 (2016, effective 2017) — this regulated trade, requiring export permits, and confirmed CITES applies to plants alongside animals.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Star Tortoise (Geochelone elegans) is listed under CITES Appendix I, making all commercial international trade in live specimens and their parts illegal.
statement_analysis.reason: Indian Star Tortoise was uplisted to CITES Appendix I at CoP17 (2016) due to massive illegal pet trade demand, making all commercial trade prohibited.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (only three correct) attracts students who know Statements 1, 3, and 4 are correct and may hesitantly accept Statement 2 (thinking 'perhaps some ivory trade was allowed for Asian elephants at some point').
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Tiger in CITES Appendix I is a foundational conservation fact; Statement 1 is correct.
Scrutinise Statement 2 — Indian Elephant is Appendix I, NOT Appendix II; the claim that commercial ivory trade is permitted is factually wrong; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — Dalbergia sissoo Appendix II listing 2017 is a specific documented fact; Statement 3 is correct.
Confirm Statement 4 — Indian Star Tortoise uplisting to Appendix I at CoP17 is documented; Statement 4 is correct.
Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — select option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits an entity-swap — substituting Appendix II for Appendix I for the Indian Elephant. This is particularly deceptive because the ongoing CITES controversy involves African Elephant ivory trade proposals (some southern African nations want Appendix II for ivory), and students who follow this debate may confuse the African trade proposals with the actual listing of the Asian/Indian Elephant, which has always been Appendix I.
solution.final_explanation:
CITES appendix membership requires species-by-species precision, especially where related species have different listings.

• Statement 1 — Correct: All tiger subspecies are Appendix I. This is the bedrock of international tiger trade prohibition.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Indian (Asian) Elephant = Appendix I. The CITES Appendix II confusion arises from the African Elephant ivory trade debate, where some southern African nations have proposed downlisting specific populations to Appendix II. India's elephant has never been in Appendix II.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Indian Rosewood is a landmark case demonstrating CITES's plant coverage. Rosewood's high value in furniture and musical instrument trade made listing necessary to control illegal logging and export.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Indian Star Tortoise is massively targeted for the international pet trade; Appendix I listing since 2016 prohibits this commercial trade.

Value Addition:
• India is one of the most active participants at CITES CoP — opposing ivory trade proposals and listing new species.
• CITES has 183 member states; it is one of the largest conservation agreements by membership.
• Over 38,000 species are protected under CITES; approximately 30,000 are plants.

solution.concept_anchor: Invasive species — not always human-introduced; CBD Article 8h scope

statement_analysis.statement: All invasive alien species in India have been introduced through direct human activity such as deliberate cultivation, cargo transport, or pet trade — natural range expansion cannot produce biologically invasive species.
statement_analysis.reason: CBD Article 8(h) and conservation science acknowledge that some species spread through natural range expansion (e.g., climate-driven shifts) and still become ecologically invasive. Policy focus is on anthropogenic introductions, but the claim that 'natural expansion cannot produce invasive species' is factually incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: The chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, identified as a major global threat to amphibians, has been documented in India's Western Ghats — one of the world's highest-diversity amphibian zones.
statement_analysis.reason: Bd (chytrid fungus) is the primary driver of global amphibian declines. Its presence has been documented in the Western Ghats, threatening India's exceptional amphibian diversity including endemic species like the Purple Frog.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) attracts students who recall that human activity drives invasive species and agree with Statement 1's overall direction without noticing the absolute qualifier 'cannot produce biologically invasive species through natural expansion.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — the claim that natural range expansion 'cannot produce biologically invasive species' is an absolute qualifier that is scientifically false; CBD Article 8(h) focuses on anthropogenic introductions but does not claim natural invasions are impossible; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — chytrid fungus presence in Western Ghats is documented and poses a threat to endemic amphibians; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap adds the absolute qualifier 'cannot produce biologically invasive species' to what sounds like a reasonable statement about human-driven invasions. CBD Article 8(h) focuses on alien species 'introduced' into ecosystems — but the word 'alien' does not preclude natural range shifts. Climate-driven expansion of species into new ranges can equally threaten native biodiversity. The statement's factual error is the absolute negation of natural invasion pathways.
solution.final_explanation:
Invasive species science and amphibian threats connect two key concepts in this question.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: While human-mediated pathways (deliberate cultivation, ballast water, pet trade, cargo) are the primary invasion routes, natural range expansion can also produce ecologically disruptive outcomes — particularly as climate change shifts species ranges. CBD Article 8(h) targets 'alien species that threaten ecosystems, habitats or species' without restricting the definition to human introductions only. The absolute 'cannot' in the statement makes it factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has caused catastrophic amphibian declines globally. Its documentation in the Western Ghats is a serious conservation concern given India's extraordinary amphibian diversity — over 400 species, many endemic. The Purple Frog's fossorial lifestyle may provide some protection, but surface-active species are more vulnerable.

Value Addition:
• Lantana camara was introduced by the British as an ornamental plant — a classic anthropogenic introduction that became India's most problematic invasive.
• Parthenium hysterophorus (congress grass) spreads naturally after initial introduction and poses dual threats — invasive and allergenic.
• A second chytrid fungus, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal), threatens salamanders globally but has not yet been confirmed in India.

statement_analysis.statement: The Hirola (Hunter's Hartebeest) is one of the 22 species covered under India's Species Recovery Programme administered by MoEFCC.
statement_analysis.reason: Hirola is a Critically Endangered African antelope found only in Kenya and Somalia — it is not an Indian species and is not part of any Indian government recovery programme. Including it exploits student unfamiliarity with the precise species list.

statement_analysis.reason: Project Dolphin announced in 2020 does cover both river dolphins (Gangetic, Indus populations) and marine dolphins — this integrated approach is a distinguishing feature of the programme.

statement_analysis.statement: The Jerdon's Courser, a nocturnal bird included in India's species recovery programme, is found primarily in Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
statement_analysis.reason: Jerdon's Courser (Rhinoptilus bitorquatus) is found in the Eastern Ghats region, specifically along the Godavari river system in Andhra Pradesh/Telangana — not in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct) attracts students who doubt Statement 2's claim about integration being a 'first' and mistakenly mark it as not correct along with Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Hirola is an African species; it cannot be part of India's recovery programme; Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 2 — Project Dolphin's dual river-marine scope is documented; while 'first' integration claim can be debated, the core fact of covering both is accurate; Statement 2 is correct and does NOT qualify as 'NOT correct'.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Jerdon's Courser is an Eastern Ghats/Godavari valley species, not Andaman & Nicobar; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a plausible-fabrication technique — Hirola is a real, well-known CR species, but it is African. UPSC sometimes inserts African or non-Indian CR species into option lists to test whether students know the specific composition of Indian programmes. A student who has memorised that 22 species are covered but not their exact names may accept Hirola as plausible because it is genuinely endangered. Statement 3 uses a geographic swap — Jerdon's Courser is a real Indian recovery species but its habitat is Eastern Ghats, not Andaman Islands.
solution.final_explanation:
India's Species Recovery Programme under MoEFCC targets 22 species including some of the most obscure and threatened in the country.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Hirola (Hunter's Hartebeest) is endemic to Kenya and Somalia. The 22 Indian species include: GIB, Snow Leopard, Dugong, Gangetic Dolphin, Manipur Brow-antlered Deer (Sangai), Jerdon's Courser, Nilgiri Tahr, Marine Turtles, Malabar Civet, Hangul, and others — all Indian species.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Project Dolphin (August 2020) integrates conservation of both river dolphins (principally Gangetic Dolphin in India's rivers) and marine dolphins in India's coastal and island waters — a unified cetacean conservation approach.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Jerdon's Courser is a nocturnal, cave-roosting bird rediscovered in 1986 after being presumed extinct. It inhabits rocky, scrub-covered terrain along the Godavari river system (Nallamala Hills, Andhra Pradesh/Telangana) — entirely unrelated to the Andaman Islands.

Value Addition:
• Jerdon's Courser is one of the world's rarest birds — fewer than 50 individuals may exist.
• The 22-species recovery programme was designed because Project Tiger and Project Elephant left many CR species without dedicated funding or management plans.
• Dugong Conservation Reserve in Gulf of Mannar (2021) is directly linked to the recovery programme.

solution.concept_anchor: WPA 2022 Amendment — schedule consolidation from 6 to 4
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (the animal must be IUCN CR to qualify for Schedule I) conflates IUCN status with WPA Schedule classification, which is the core trap of this scenario.
elimination_logic: The scenario's key question: does Schedule I protection require IUCN CR status? — No; WPA Schedule I is determined by domestic legislative process, not IUCN classification.
Eliminate option b — Schedule I listing under WPA is independent of IUCN status; Mugger Crocodile is LC but Schedule I; Bengal Tiger is EN not CR but Schedule I.
Eliminate option c — WPA 2022 reduced schedules from 6 to 4; there is no Schedule VI since the amendment.
Eliminate option d — the State Government cannot modify Schedule classification; only Parliament can amend the schedules of WPA.
Select option a — Schedule I protection under WPA is determined solely by domestic law (WPA 1972 as amended); IUCN status is irrelevant to this determination.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to trigger the Schedule I = IUCN CR conflation. A student who has absorbed the false equivalence between maximum domestic protection and maximum international threat classification will choose option b. The correct principle — that WPA Schedule classification is entirely a domestic legislative matter decided by Parliament, independent of IUCN scientific assessments — is the applied concept.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the independence of WPA Schedule classification from IUCN Red List status.

Applicable principle: Schedule I of WPA 1972 is determined by Parliament through domestic legislation. The inclusion of a species in Schedule I reflects India's legislative judgment about the level of protection needed — it does not require the species to be IUCN CR or any particular IUCN category.

• Option (a) — Correct: WPA Schedule I confers the highest legal protection regardless of IUCN status. Species are placed in Schedule I based on Parliament's assessment; a legally valid Schedule I listing stands on its own domestic authority.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: This is the core conflation trap. IUCN status and WPA Schedule are parallel but independent systems. Mugger Crocodile (IUCN LC) is Schedule I; Bengal Tiger (IUCN EN, not CR) is Schedule I. The officer's reasoning is legally invalid.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The WPA Amendment 2022 eliminated Schedule VI (previously the prohibited plants list) by reorganising into 4 schedules. There is no Schedule VI post-2022.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: WPA Schedule modifications require Parliamentary amendment — state governments have no power to change which schedule a species falls under.

Value Addition:
• Post-2022 WPA: Schedule I (highest protection), Schedule II (protected but lower penalty), Schedule III (aquatic invertebrates), Schedule IV (plants).
• The government can grant special permission for certain activities involving Schedule I species for scientific research or captive breeding.
• India's domestic WPA classification may be more or less protective than IUCN suggests — legislative wisdom and scientific assessment operate independently.

solution.final_explanation:
The Great Indian Bustard sits at the intersection of species conservation, geography, and energy policy.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: GIB is primarily a Rajasthan species but not exclusively. Maharashtra's Solapur district (Nanaj sanctuary area) and Karnataka's Ranebennur Blackbuck Sanctuary area host smaller confirmed populations. Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh also have occasional sightings of small resident groups. The 'only Rajasthan' claim fails geographic precision.
• Statement 2 — Correct: GIB's single-egg clutch means that even in successful captive breeding conditions, population growth is inherently slow. This makes every individual — and every egg — critical. The Sam breeding centre's progress has been closely monitored for this reason.
• Statement 3 — Correct: India's National Solar Mission targets significant solar energy capacity; Rajasthan's Thar is optimal for this. The same desert is GIB's last viable habitat. The Supreme Court's 2021 direction on underground cabling directly acknowledged this conflict — a rare judicial recognition of inter-SDG tension.

Value Addition:
• GIB was once found across 11 Indian states; its range has contracted to fragments in fewer than 5.
• Weight: up to 15 kg — one of the world's heaviest flying birds; flight capability limits its ability to dodge power lines.
• The 'Bustard' in the name comes from the Latin 'avis tarda' (slow bird) — ironic given its conservation urgency.
